spl_patient_package_insert: PATIENT INFORMATION NovoLog ® Mix 70/30 (NŌ-vō-log-MIX-SEV-en-tee-THIR-tee) (insulin aspart protamine and insulin aspart) injectable suspension, for subcutaneous use Do not share your NovoLog Mix 70/30 FlexPen with other people, even if the needle has been changed. You may give other people a serious infection, or get a serious infection from them. What is NovoLog Mix 70/30? NovoLog Mix 70/30 is a man-made insulin that is used to control high blood sugar in people with diabetes mellitus. It is not known if NovoLog Mix 70/30 is safe and effective in children. Who should not take NovoLog Mix 70/30? Do not take NovoLog Mix 70/30 if you: are having an episode of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). have an allergy to NovoLog Mix 70/30 or any of the ingredients in NovoLog Mix 70/30. Before taking NovoLog Mix 70/30, tell your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions including, if you are: pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or are breastfeeding. taking new prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. Before you start taking NovoLog Mix 70/30, talk to your healthcare provider about low blood sugar and how to manage it. How should I take NovoLog Mix 70/30? Read the Instructions for Use that come with your NovoLog Mix 70/30. Take NovoLog Mix 70/30 exactly as your healthcare provider tells you to. NovoLog Mix 70/30 starts acting fast. If you have Type 1 diabetes, inject it up to 15 minutes before you eat a meal. Do not inject NovoLog Mix 70/30 if you are not planning to eat within 15 minutes. If you have Type 2 diabetes, you may inject NovoLog Mix 70/30 up to 15 minutes before or after starting your meal. Do not mix NovoLog Mix 70/30 with other insulin products or use in an insulin pump. Know the type and strength of insulin you take. Do not change the type of insulin you take unless your healthcare provider tells you to. The amount of insulin and the best time for you to take your insulin may need to change if you take different types of insulin. Check your blood sugar levels. Ask your healthcare provider what your blood sugars should be and when you should check your blood sugar levels. Do not reuse or share your needles or syringes with other people. You may give other people a serious infection or get a serious infection from them. NovoLog Mix 70/30 is injected under the skin (subcutaneously) of your stomach area, buttocks, upper legs, or upper arms. Change (rotate) your injection sites within the same area you choose with each dose to reduce your risk of getting lipodystrophy (pits in skin or thickened skin) and localized cutaneous amyloidosis (skin with lumps) at the injection sites. Do not use the exact same spot for each injection. Do not inject where skin has pits, is thickened, or has lumps. Do not inject where the skin is tender, bruised, scaly or hard, or into scars or damaged skin. What should I avoid while taking NovoLog Mix 70/30? While taking NovoLog Mix 70/30 do not: Drive or operate heavy machinery, until you know how NovoLog Mix 70/30 affects you. Drink alcohol or use prescription or over-the-counter medicines that contain alcohol. What are the possible side effects of NovoLog Mix 70/30? NovoLog Mix 70/30 may cause serious side effects that can lead to death, including: Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Signs and symptoms that may indicate low blood sugar include: dizziness or light-headedness blurred vision anxiety, irritability, or mood changes sweating slurred speech hunger confusion shakiness headache fast heart beat Your insulin dose may need to change because of: change in level of physical activity or exercise increased stress change in diet weight gain or loss illness Other common side effects of NovoLog Mix 70/30 may include: low potassium in your blood (hypokalemia), reactions at the injection site, itching, rash, serious allergic reactions (whole body reactions), skin thickening or pits at the injection site (lipodystrophy), weight gain, and swelling of your hands and feet. Get emergency medical help if you have: trouble breathing, shortness of breath, fast heartbeat, swelling of your face, tongue, or throat, sweating, extreme drowsiness, dizziness, confusion. These are not all the possible side effects of NovoLog Mix 70/30. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088. General information about the safe and effective use of NovoLog Mix 70/30. Medicines are sometimes prescribed for purposes other than those listed in a Patient Information leaflet. You can ask your pharmacist or healthcare provider for information about NovoLog Mix 70/30 that is written for health professionals. Do not use NovoLog Mix 70/30 for a condition for which it was not prescribed. Do not give NovoLog Mix 70/30 to other people, even if they have the same symptoms that you have. It may harm them. What are the ingredients in NovoLog Mix 70/30? Active Ingredient: 70% insulin aspart protamine and 30% insulin aspart. Inactive Ingredients : disodium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate, glycerol, metacresol, phenol, protamine sulfate, sodium chloride, zinc, and Water for Injection, USP. Hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide may be added to adjust pH. This Patient Information has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Revised: 2/2023 INSTRUCTIONS FOR USE NovoLog ® Mix 70/30 (insulin aspart protamine and insulin aspart) injectable suspension, for subcutaneous use 10 mL multiple-dose vial (100 Units/mL, U-100) Read this Instructions for Use before you start taking NovoLog Mix 70/30 and each time you get a refill. There may be new information. This information does not take the place of talking to your healthcare provider about your medical condition or your treatment. Supplies you will need to give your NovoLog Mix 70/30 injection: 10 mL NovoLog Mix 70/30 vial insulin syringe and needle alcohol swabs Preparing your NovoLog Mix 70/30 dose: Wash your hands with soap and water. Before you start to prepare your injection, check the NovoLog Mix 70/30 label to make sure that you are taking the right type of insulin. This is especially important if you use more than 1 type of insulin. NovoLog Mix 70/30 should look white and cloudy after mixing. Do not use NovoLog Mix 70/30 if it looks clear or contains any lumps or particles. NovoLog Mix 70/30 is easier to mix when it is at room temperature. After mixing NovoLog Mix 70/30, inject your dose right away. If you wait to inject your dose, the insulin will need to be mixed again. Do not use NovoLog Mix 70/30 past the expiration date printed on the label. Step 1: If you are using a new vial, pull off the tamper-resistant cap (See Figure A). Step 2: Wipe the rubber stopper with an alcohol swab (See Figure B). Step 3: Roll the NovoLog Mix 70/30 vial between your hands 10 times. Keep the vial in a horizontal (flat) position (See Figure C). Roll the vial between your hands until the NovoLog Mix 70/30 looks white and cloudy. Do not shake the vial. Step 4: Hold the syringe with the needle pointing up. Pull down on the plunger until the black tip reaches the line for the number of units for your prescribed dose (See Figure D). Step 5: Push the needle through the rubber stopper of the NovoLog Mix 70/30 vial (See Figure E). Step 6: Push the plunger all the way in. This puts air into the NovoLog Mix 70/30 vial (See Figure F). Step 7: Turn the NovoLog Mix 70/30 vial and syringe upside down and slowly pull the plunger down until the black tip is a few units past the line for your dose (See Figure G). If there are air bubbles, tap the syringe gently a few times to let any air bubbles rise to the top (See Figure H). Step 8: Slowly push the plunger up until the black tip reaches the line for your NovoLog Mix 70/30 dose (See Figure I). Step 9: Check the syringe to make sure you have the right dose of NovoLog Mix 70/30. Step 10: Pull the syringe out of the vial’s rubber stopper (See Figure J). Giving your injection: Inject your NovoLog Mix 70/30 exactly as your healthcare provider has shown you. Your healthcare provider should tell you if you need to pinch the skin before injecting. NovoLog Mix 70/30 is injected under the skin (subcutaneously) of your stomach area, buttocks, upper legs, or upper arms. Change (rotate) your injection sites within the area you choose for each dose to reduce your risk of getting lipodystrophy (pits in skin or thickened skin) and localized cutaneous amyloidosis (skin with lumps) at the injection sites. Do not use the same injection site for each injection. Do not inject where the skin has pits, thickened, or has lumps. Do not inject where the skin is tender, bruised, scaly or hard, or into scars or damaged skin. Step 11: Choose your injection site and wipe the skin with an alcohol swab. Let the injection site dry before you inject your dose (See Figure K). Step 12: Insert the needle into your skin. Push down on the plunger to inject your dose (See Figure L). The needle should remain in the skin for at least 6 seconds to make sure you have injected all the insulin. Step 13: Pull the needle out of your skin. After that, you may see a drop of NovoLog Mix 70/30 at the needle tip. This is normal and does not affect the dose you just received (See Figure M). If you see blood after you take the needle out of your skin, press the injection site lightly with a piece of gauze or an alcohol swab. Do not rub the area. After your injection: Do not recap the needle. Recapping the needle can lead to a needle stick injury. Put the empty insulin vials, used needles and syringes in a FDA-cleared sharps disposal container right away after use. Do not throw away (dispose of) loose needles and syringes in your household trash. If you do not have a FDA-cleared sharps disposal container, you may use a household container that is: made of a heavy-duty plastic, can be closed with a tight-fitting, puncture-resistant lid, without sharps being able to come out, upright and stable during use, leak-resistant, and properly labeled to warn of hazardous waste inside the container. When your sharps disposal container is almost full, you will need to follow your community guidelines for the right way to dispose of your sharps disposal container. There may be state or local laws about how you should throw away used needles and syringes. For more information about the safe sharps disposal, and for specific information about sharps disposal in the state that you live in, go to the FDA’s website at: http://www.fda.gov/safesharpsdisposal . Do not dispose of your used sharps disposal container in your household trash unless your community guidelines permit this. Do not recycle your used sharps disposal container. How should I store NovoLog Mix 70/30? Do not freeze NovoLog Mix 70/30. Do not use NovoLog Mix 70/30 if it has been frozen. Keep NovoLog Mix 70/30 away from heat or light. All unopened vials: Store unopened NovoLog Mix 70/30 vials in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Unopened vials may be used until the expiration date printed on the label, if they have been stored in the refrigerator. Unopened vials should be thrown away after 28 days, if they are stored at room temperature. After vials have been opened: Opened NovoLog Mix 70/30 vials can be stored in the refrigerator 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C) or at room temperature below 86°F (30°C) for up to 28 days. Throw away all opened NovoLog Mix 70/30 vials after 28 days, even if they still have insulin left in them. General information about the safe and effective use of NovoLog Mix 70/30 Always use a new syringe and needle for each injection. Do not share syringes or needles. Keep NovoLog Mix 70/30 vials, syringes, and needles out of the reach of children. This Instructions for Use has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. indications_and_usage: 1 INDICATIONS AND USAGE ONSWIK™ is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. ONSWIK™ is a long-acting insulin analog indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. ( 1 ) Limitations of Use: Not recommended for use in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus due to increased risk of severe hypoglycemia ( 1 ) Limitations of Use ONSWIK is not recommended for use in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus due to increased risk of severe hypoglycemia. [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 )] .
dosage_and_administration: 2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION See Full Prescribing Information for general dosing and important administration instructions. ( 2.1 , 2.2 ) Administer once weekly on the same day each week. The scheduled injection day may be changed, provided 4 days have elapsed since the last dose. Once the injection day is changed, continue administering ONSWIK on the new chosen day. ( 2.1 ) Individualize and adjust the dosage based on metabolic needs, glucose monitoring results and glycemic control goal. ( 2.1 ) Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen, upper arm, thigh, or buttocks. ( 2.2 ) Rotate injection sites to reduce risk of lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis. ( 2.2 ) May administer alone or in any combination with oral and injectable antidiabetic medicines and bolus insulin. ( 2.2 ) See Full Prescribing Information for recommended starting dosage in insulin naïve patients and patients already on a daily basal insulin. ( 2.3 , 2.4 ) 2.1 General Dosing Instructions ONSWIK is available as a single-patient-use prefilled pen (KwikPen) in 2 concentrations (U-500 and U-1,000). The U-500 KwikPen delivers doses in 5-unit increments and can deliver up to 400 units in a single injection. The U-1,000 KwikPen delivers doses in 10-unit increments and can deliver up to 800 units in a single injection. Administer ONSWIK by subcutaneous injection once weekly on the same day each week. If necessary, the scheduled injection day may be changed, provided at least 4 days have elapsed since the last dose. Once the injection day is changed, continue administering ONSWIK on the new chosen day. Do not repeat administration of the one-time starting dose [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.6 ), Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Individualize and adjust the dosage of ONSWIK based on metabolic needs, glucose monitoring results and glycemic control goal. If glycemic control does not improve despite adherence to diet, medication adherence, and escalating dosages of ONSWIK, consider switching to another insulin product [see Immunogenicity ( 12.6 )] . The potency of insulin analogs, including ONSWIK, is expressed in units. One ( 1 ) unit of ONSWIK corresponds to 1 international unit of human insulin. Consider the long half-life of ONSWIK when adjusting the dosage. When the dosage is adjusted, initial changes in fasting blood glucose (FBG) are expected within 1 to 2 weeks, with the full treatment effect of the dosage adjustment occurring in approximately 4 weeks [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 , 12.3 )] . Dosage adjustment is not recommended during acute illness nor when patients make short-term changes in their physical activity level or usual diet. In these situations, consider other applicable adjustments, e.g., glucose intake or changes to other glucose lowering medication [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 , 12.3 )] . 2.2 Important Administration Instructions Always check insulin labels before administration [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . Inspect ONSWIK visually before use. Only use ONSWIK if the solution is clear and colorless to yellow with no visible particles. Prior to initiation, train patients and their caregiver(s) on how to select their weekly ONSWIK dosage. Instruct patients to visually verify the dialed units on the dose window of the ONSWIK KwikPen before each injection to avoid dosing errors, including underdosage and overdosage, that may lead to hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, respectively. Inject ONSWIK subcutaneously into the abdomen, upper arm, thigh, or buttocks. Rotate injection sites within the same region from one injection to the next to reduce the risk of lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis. Do not inject into areas of lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 ), Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )] . During changes to a patient's insulin regimen, increase the frequency of glucose monitoring [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 )] . Use ONSWIK prefilled pen products with caution in patients with visual impairment who may rely on audible clicks to dial their dose. ONSWIK may be administered alone or in any combination with oral and injectable antidiabetic medicines and rapid-acting or short-acting insulin products. Do not administer ONSWIK intramuscularly, intravenously or in an insulin pump. Do not dilute or mix ONSWIK with any insulin product or other solutions. Do not transfer ONSWIK from the prefilled pen to a syringe for administration [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] . 2.3 Recommended Dosage in Insulin Naïve Patients There are two dosing options for insulin naïve patients: a fixed-dosage titration and a flexible-dosage titration. Fixed-Dosage Titration The recommended starting dosage is 100 units injected subcutaneously once weekly on the same day each week. After a minimum of 4 weeks, titrate the dosage based on the patient's metabolic needs, glucose monitoring results and glycemic goal according to Table 1 . Table 1: Fixed-Dosage Titration Dosing Dosage (units) once weekly Recommended starting dosage 100 After a minimum of 4 weeks on a stable dose, if the fasting glycemic goal has not been reached and the FBG is above 130 mg/dL, titrate sequentially to the next higher dose shown on the right. If the patient experiences hypoglycemia within the prior week, withhold further dosage increases until the cause has been addressed and hypoglycemia has resolved. 150 250 400 If the FBG is below 130 mg/dL and the fasting glycemic goal has not been reached, titrate the dosage by 20 to 40 units per week as necessary. If a dosage greater than 400 units once weekly is required to reach glycemic goal, titrate the dosage by 20 to 40 units per week as necessary. Flexible-Dosage Titration See Table 2 for dosage and important considerations for the flexible-dosage titration. Table 2: Flexible-Dosage Titration Week Dosage (units) Important Considerations First week 300 The 300-unit One-Time Starting Dose is only administered during the first week. Second week 100 Do not repeat the 300-unit One-Time Starting Dose. Third and subsequent weeks Adjust the ONSWIK dosage by 20 units to 40 units per week. Titrate the dosage as necessary based on the patient's fasting glycemic goal. 2.4 Switching from Once- or Twice-Daily Basal Insulin to ONSWIK Administer the first dose of ONSWIK on the day after the last dose of once- or twice-daily basal insulin. Close glucose monitoring is recommended during the switch and until the dosage and glycemic control are stable. Doses and timing of concurrent mealtime insulin products or other concomitant antidiabetic medications may require adjustments. See Table 3 for dosage calculations and important considerations when switching patients from once- or twice-daily basal insulin to ONSWIK. Table 3: Switching From Once- or Twice-Daily Basal Insulin to ONSWIK a Round calculated doses to the nearest 5 units for the U-500 KwikPen and 10 units for the U-1,000 KwikPen. b For patients switching from once-daily insulin glargine 300 units/mL or twice-daily NPH insulin to ONSWIK, use 80% of the total daily insulin glargine or NPH insulin dosage when calculating ONSWIK dosages. Weekly Dosage Dosage Calculation (units) a Important Considerations First week One-Time Starting Dose: Multiply the total daily basal b insulin dosage by 7, then multiply by 3. The One - Time Starting Dose is only administered during the first week. For patients who have FBG values less than or equal to 120 mg/dL on daily basal insulin: Consider omitting the One-Time Starting Dose. Instead, the first week dose is the total daily basal b insulin dosage multiplied by 7 If the One-Time Starting Dose is omitted: Transient hyperglycemia may occur and last 4 to 6 weeks. Second week Multiply the previous total daily basal b insulin dosage by 7 Do not repeat the One-Time Starting Dose. Third and subsequent weeks Adjust the ONSWIK dosage by 20 units to 40 units per week, as necessary based on the fasting glycemic goal. If the One-Time Starting Dose was omitted: Do not adjust the weekly dosage of ONSWIK until FBG levels have stabilized. If the FBG level is stable and remains above the goal, the dosage may be adjusted, as necessary based on the patient's fasting glycemic goal. 2.5 Recommendations Regarding Missed Dose If a dose is missed: Administer the missed dose as soon as possible within 4 days of the missed dose then maintain the regular weekly dosing schedule. If more than 4 days have passed there are two options. Patients can skip the missed dose and administer the usual dose on the regularly scheduled day. Alternatively, patients can administer the missed dose then resume the once-weekly dosing schedule, one week from the day the missed dose was administered. Increase blood glucose monitoring with missed dosage. 2.6 Management of Accidental Extra Dose(s) If the one-time starting dose is accidentally administered more than once (for example, if the one-time starting dose is administered for 2 consecutive weeks), skip the next week's dose. If the weekly dosage is administered more than once in the same week, skip the next week's dose. Monitor glucose levels more frequently and assess for repeated or severe hypoglycemia.

warnings_and_cautions: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Hypoglycemia Due to Medication Errors and Accidental Overdose: Accidental mix-ups between insulin products can occur. Advise patients to always check the product label before each injection to confirm they are using ONSWIK and not another insulin or injectable antidiabetic medicine. Do not transfer ONSWIK into a syringe as overdosage and severe hypoglycemia can result. Do not repeat the one-time starting dose after the first injection. ( 5.1 ) Hypoglycemia: May be life-threatening. Increase frequency of glucose monitoring with changes to insulin dosage, co-administered glucose-lowering medications, meal pattern, physical activity, and in patients with renal impairment or hepatic impairment or hypoglycemia unawareness. ( 5.3 ) Hyperglycemia or Hypoglycemia with changes in insulin regimen: Make changes to a patient's insulin regimen (e.g., insulin strength, manufacturer, type, injection site or method of administration) under close medical supervision with increased frequency of glucose monitoring. ( 5.4 ) Hypersensitivity Reactions: Severe, life-threatening, generalized allergy, including anaphylaxis, can occur. Discontinue ONSWIK, monitor and treat if indicated. ( 5.5 ) Hypokalemia: May be life-threatening. Monitor potassium levels in patients at risk for hypokalemia and treat if indicated. ( 5.6 ) Never share ONSWIK between patients, even if the needle is changed. ( 5.7 ) Fluid Retention and Heart Failure with Concomitant Use of PPAR-Gamma Agonists: Observe for signs and symptoms of heart failure; consider dosage reduction or discontinuation of the PPAR-gamma agonist if heart failure occurs. ( 5.8 ) 5.1 Hypoglycemia Due to Medication Errors and Accidental Overdose Serious hypoglycemia requiring hospitalization has occurred due to accidental mix-ups between once-weekly insulin products and other insulin products or once-weekly injectable antidiabetic medicines, incorrect dose selection, and dosing frequency errors. To avoid dosing errors when switching from daily basal insulin to ONSWIK, follow the dosage recommendations in the Dosage and Administration Section ( 2.4 ). Administer ONSWIK once weekly only. Do not repeat administration of the one-time starting dose. Advise patients to always check the product label before each injection to confirm they are using ONSWIK and not another insulin or injectable antidiabetic medicine. Prior to initiation, train patients and their caregiver(s) on how to select their weekly ONSWIK dosage. Advise patients using other injectable medications for glycemic control that the dosage selection of ONSWIK differs. Instruct patients to visually verify the dialed units on the dose window of the ONSWIK KwikPen before each injection to avoid dosing errors. Patients should not dial the maximum single dose (400 units for the U-500 KwikPen or 800 units for the U-1,000 KwikPen) of ONSWIK unless this is the prescribed dose Patients should not use a syringe to remove ONSWIK from the ONSWIK KwikPen. The markings on the syringe will not measure the dose correctly and this can result in overdosage and severe hypoglycemia [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.2 , 2.3 , 2.4 ), Instructions for Use] . Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, particularly during the first several weeks after initiation or dose escalation of ONSWIK. Ensure patients understand how to recognize and manage hypoglycemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )]. 5.2 Severe Hypoglycemia in Patients with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus ONSWIK is not recommended for use in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus due to increased risk of severe hypoglycemia. In a 52-week clinical trial of adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus, the incidence of Level 3 (severe) hypoglycemia was higher for patients treated with ONSWIK compared with insulin degludec (10% versus 3%). 5.3 Hypoglycemia Hypoglycemia is the most common adverse reaction associated with insulins, including ONSWIK [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )] . Severe hypoglycemia can cause seizures, may lead to unconsciousness, may be life-threatening, or cause death. Hypoglycemia can impair concentration ability and reaction time; this may place an individual and others at risk in situations where these abilities are important (e.g., driving or operating other machinery). Hypoglycemia can happen suddenly, and symptoms may differ in each individual and change over time in the same individual. Symptomatic awareness of hypoglycemia may be less pronounced in patients with longstanding diabetes, in patients with diabetic nerve disease, in patients using medications that block the sympathetic nervous system (e.g., beta-blockers) [see Drug Interactions ( 7 )] , or in patients who experience recurrent hypoglycemia. The long-acting effect of ONSWIK may delay recovery from hypoglycemia compared to shorter-acting insulins [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 , 12.3 )] . Risk Factors for Hypoglycemia The risk of hypoglycemia generally increases with intensity of glycemic control. The risk of hypoglycemia after an injection is related to the duration of action of the insulin [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 )] and, in general, is highest when the glucose lowering effect of the insulin is maximal. As with all insulins, the glucose lowering effect over time of ONSWIK may vary among different individuals or at different times in the same individual and depends on many conditions, including the area of injection as well as the injection site blood supply and temperature. Other factors that may increase the risk of hypoglycemia include changes in meal pattern (e.g., macronutrient content or timing of meals), changes in level of physical activity, or changes to co-administered medication [see Drug Interactions ( 7 ) ] . Patients with renal or hepatic impairment may be at higher risk of hypoglycemia [see Use in Specific Populations ( 8.6 , 8.7 )]. Risk Mitigation Strategies for Hypoglycemia Educate patients and caregivers to recognize and manage hypoglycemia. Self-monitoring of blood glucose plays an essential role in the prevention and management of hypoglycemia. In patients at higher risk for hypoglycemia and patients who have reduced symptomatic awareness of hypoglycemia, increased frequency of blood glucose monitoring is recommended. 5.4 Hyperglycemia or Hypoglycemia with Changes in Insulin Regimen Changes in an insulin regimen (e.g., insulin strength, manufacturer, type, injection site or method of administration) may affect glycemic control and predispose to hypoglycemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )] or hyperglycemia. Repeated insulin injections into areas of lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis have been reported to result in hyperglycemia; and a sudden change in the injection site (to an unaffected area) has been reported to result in hypoglycemia [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )]. The risk of hyperglycemia may be increased during the first four to six weeks of titration, especially if ONSWIK is initiated without the one-time starting dose [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.3 , 2.4 ), Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 , 12.3 )] . Make any changes to a patient's insulin regimen under close medical supervision with increased frequency of glucose monitoring. Advise patients who have repeatedly injected into areas of lipodystrophy or localized cutaneous amyloidosis to change the injection site to unaffected areas and closely monitor for hypoglycemia. Adjustments in concomitant anti-diabetic treatment may be needed [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.3 , 2.4 )]. 5.5 Hypersensitivity Reactions Severe, life-threatening, generalized allergy, including anaphylaxis, can occur with insulins, including ONSWIK [see Adverse Reactions ( 6.1 )] . If hypersensitivity reactions occur, discontinue ONSWIK; treat per standard of care and monitor until symptoms and signs resolve. ONSWIK is contraindicated in patients who have had hypersensitivity reactions to insulin efsitora alfa-gobe or any of the excipients in ONSWIK [see Contraindications ( 4 )] . 5.6 Hypokalemia All insulins, including ONSWIK, cause a shift in potassium from the extracellular to intracellular space, possibly leading to hypokalemia. Untreated hypokalemia may cause respiratory paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia, and death. Monitor potassium levels in patients at risk for hypokalemia (e.g., patients using potassium-lowering medications, patients taking medications sensitive to serum potassium concentrations) and treat if indicated. 5.7 Never Share an ONSWIK Prefilled Pen Between Patients ONSWIK prefilled pens must never be shared between patients, even if the needle is changed. Sharing poses a risk for transmission of blood-borne pathogens. 5.8 Fluid Retention and Heart Failure with Concomitant Use of PPAR-Gamma Agonists Thiazolidinediones (TZDs), which are peroxisome proliferator activated receptor (PPAR)-gamma agonists, can cause dose-related fluid retention, when used in combination with insulin. Fluid retention may lead to or exacerbate heart failure. Patients treated with insulin, including ONSWIK and a PPAR-gamma agonist should be observed for signs and symptoms of heart failure. If heart failure develops, it should be managed according to current standards of care and discontinuation or dose reduction of the PPAR-gamma agonist must be considered.
adverse_reactions: 6 ADVERSE REACTIONS The following adverse reactions are described below or elsewhere in the prescribing information: Hypoglycemia Due to Medication Errors and Accidental Overdose [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Severe Hypoglycemia in Patients with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 )] . Hypoglycemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )] . Hypersensitivity Reactions [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.5 )] . Hypokalemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.6 )]. Common adverse reactions include hypoglycemia, hypersensitivity reactions, injection site reactions, lipodystrophy, pruritus, rash, edema, and weight gain. ( 6.1 ) To report SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTIONS, contact Eli Lilly and Company at 1-800-LillyRx (1-800-545-5979) or FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch. 6.1 Clinical Trials Experience Because clinical trials are conducted under widely varying conditions, adverse reaction rates observed in the clinical trials of a drug cannot be directly compared to rates in the clinical trials of another drug and may not reflect the rates observed in clinical practice. The safety of ONSWIK was evaluated in four clinical trials involving 1,883 adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus exposed to ONSWIK, with a mean exposure duration of 372 days [see Clinical Studies ( 14 )] . The mean age was 59 years, the mean duration of diabetes was 13 years, 55% were male, 63% were White, 21% were Asian, 10% were American Indian or Alaska Native, 5% were Black or African American, and 45% were Hispanic. The mean BMI was 31 kg/m 2 and the mean HbA1c at baseline was 8.1%. Common Adverse Reactions Hypoglycemia Hypoglycemia is the most common adverse reaction in patients using insulin, including ONSWIK. The frequency of reported hypoglycemia depends on the definition of hypoglycemia used, diabetes type, insulin dose, intensity of glucose control, background therapies, and other intrinsic and extrinsic patient factors. For these reasons, comparing the frequency of hypoglycemia in clinical trials for ONSWIK with the frequency of hypoglycemia for other products may be misleading and may not be representative of hypoglycemia frequencies that occur in clinical practice. In clinical trials [see Clinical Studies ( 14 )], events of severe hypoglycemia (level 3) were defined as an episode associated with severe cognitive impairment requiring external assistance for recovery. Hypoglycemia episodes with a glucose level below 54 mg/dL with or without associated symptoms (level 2 hypoglycemia) were also assessed in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. In clinical trials in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, the proportions of adults treated with ONSWIK who experienced at least one episode of level 3 and/or level 2 hypoglycemia in clinical trials are shown in Table 4 . Allergic Reactions Severe, life-threatening, generalized allergy, including anaphylaxis, generalized skin reactions, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, and shock may occur with any insulin, including ONSWIK. Hypersensitivity reactions were reported in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK: contact dermatitis (0.7%), rash (0.7%), dermatitis (0.7%), hypersensitivity (0.6%), pruritus (0.6%), eczema (0.6%) and allergic rhinitis (0.5%). Lipodystrophy was reported in 0.3% of adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with ONSWIK without mealtime insulin therapy gained an average of 2.1 to 3.9 kg after 52 weeks of treatment. use_in_specific_populations: 8 USE IN SPECIFIC POPULATIONS Pregnancy: Use during pregnancy is not recommended. ( 8.1 ) Lactation: Use during breastfeeding or lactation is not recommended. ( 8.2 ) 8.1 Pregnancy Risk Summary The use of ONSWIK during pregnancy is not recommended. Available data with ONSWIK use in pregnant women are insufficient to evaluate for a drug-related risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. There are risks to the mother and fetus associated with poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy ( see Clinical Considerations ). Based on animal reproduction studies, there may be risks to the fetus from exposure to ONSWIK during pregnancy. In pregnant rats or rabbits administered insulin efsitora alfa-gobe during organogenesis, early embryonic deaths, and fetal abnormalities occurred at clinically relevant exposures at the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) of 1,400 units /week and were associated with hypoglycemia in maternal non-diabetic animals. Hypoglycemia-related mortality occurred in rats during pregnancy and following birth, and pup mortality occurred during the lactation period, which correlated with plasma exposure levels of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe and severe hypoglycemia in pups. Human IgG is known to cross the placental barrier via FcRn transfer; therefore, insulin efsitora alfa-gobe may be transmitted from the mother to the developing fetus in late pregnancy. The estimated background risk of major birth defects is 6% to 10% in women with pre - gestational diabetes with a HbA1c>7% and has been reported to be as high as 20% to 25% in women with a HbA1c >10%. The estimated background risk of miscarriage for the indicated population is unknown. In the U.S. general population, the estimated background risk of major birth defects and miscarriage in clinically recognized pregnancies is 2% to 4% and 15% to 20%, respectively. Clinical Considerations Disease-associated Maternal and/or Embryo-Fetal Risk Poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy increases the maternal risk for diabetic ketoacidosis, pre - eclampsia, spontaneous abortions, preterm delivery, and delivery complications. Poorly controlled diabetes increases the fetal risk for major birth defects, stillbirth, and macrosomia related morbidity. Data Animal Data In pregnant rats, insulin efsitora alfa-gobe did not cause adverse effects on embryo-fetal development when given subcutaneously during organogenesis at doses of 22 and 75 units/kg/week, which were up to 0.2-fold the MRHD, based on AUC. However, increased post-implantation loss secondary to maternal hypoglycemia was observed when rats were given 75 units/kg/week insulin efsitora alfa-gobe prior to and during mating and through early gestation (Gestation Day 6) at clinically relevant exposures. In pregnant rabbits given subcutaneous doses during organogenesis of 6 and 22 units/kg/week insulin efsitora alfa-gobe weekly, which were up to 0.1-fold the MRHD, post-implantation losses and fetal skeletal/visceral abnormalities were observed at clinically relevant exposures, which were secondary to maternal hypoglycemia. In a pre- and postnatal developmental study in rats where insulin efsitora alfa-gobe was given subcutaneously from implantation through the end of lactation (Gestation Day 6 through Lactation Day 20) at doses of 22 and 75 units/kg/week, which were up to 0.6-fold the MRHD, hypoglycemia-related maternal mortality during or following birth and pup mortality during the lactation period occurred at clinically relevant exposures. There was plasma exposure of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe and severe hypoglycemia in pups, which is likely due to FcRn-mediated transfer of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe. 8.2 Lactation Risk Summary The use of ONSWIK during breastfeeding or lactation is not recommended. There are no data on the presence of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe in animal or human milk, the effects on the breastfed infant, or the effects on milk production. Based on plasma exposure levels of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe in rat pups, there is indirect evidence of presence of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe in the milk. 8.4 Pediatric Use Safety and effectiveness of ONSWIK have not been established in pediatric patients. ONSWIK is not recommended for use in pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus due to increased risk of severe hypoglycemia [ see Indications and Usage ( 1 ) and Warnings and Precautions ( 5.2 ) ]. 8.5 Geriatric Use In clinical trials, 30% (561/1,883) of ONSWIK - treated patients were 65 years of age or older, and 5% (85/1,883) of ONSWIK - treated patients were 75 years of age or older at baseline. No overall differences in safety or effectiveness of ONSWIK have been observed between patients 65 years of age and older and younger adult patients. Greater caution should be exercised when ONSWIK is administered to geriatric patients since greater sensitivity of some older individuals to the effects of ONSWIK cannot be ruled out. The initial dosing, dose increments, and maintenance dosage should be conservative to avoid hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia may be more difficult to recognize in the elderly. More frequent glucose monitoring is recommended, and the insulin dose is to be adjusted on an individual basis. 8.6 Renal Impairment No clinically relevant differences in the pharmacokinetics of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe were observed across the different renal impairment subgroups [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )] . Additional dose adjustment should not be necessary for patients with renal impairment. However, as with all insulin products, glucose monitoring should be intensified and the ONSWIK dosage adjusted on an individual basis in patients with renal impairment. 8.7 Hepatic Impairment No difference in the pharmacokinetics of ONSWIK was identified comparing healthy subjects and subjects with hepatic impairment [see Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.3 )] . Additional dose adjustment should not be necessary for patients with hepatic impairment. However, as with all insulin products, glucose monitoring should be intensified and the ONSWIK dosage adjusted on an individual basis in patients with hepatic impairment.

overdosage: 10 OVERDOSAGE Overdosage of insulin may cause hypoglycemia with accompanying symptoms that include listlessness, confusion, palpitations, sweating, vomiting, and headache. Hypoglycemia and hypokalemia may occur as a result of an excess of ONSWIK relative to food intake, energy expenditure, or both [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 , 5.6 )]. Mild episodes of hypoglycemia usually can be treated with oral carbohydrates. Lowering the dosage of ONSWIK, adjustments in meal patterns, or physical activity may be needed. More severe episodes with coma, seizure, or neurologic impairment may be treated with glucagon or concentrated intravenous glucose. Sustained carbohydrate intake and observation may be necessary, because hypoglycemia may recur after apparent clinical recovery. Hypokalemia must be corrected appropriately. Consideration of the prolonged duration of action of ONSWIK is recommended in the management of overdose [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.6 ), Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 ), Clinical Pharmacology ( 12.2 )] .
description: 11 DESCRIPTION Insulin efsitora alfa - gobe is a long-acting insulin analog that is divalent (dimer), consisting of a single - chain insulin (comprised of insulin B - chain analog, a short peptide linker, and an insulin A - chain analog) fused to a second peptide linker that is fused to a human IgG2 Fc region. Each monomer is comprised of 299 amino acid residues. Insulin efsitora alfa - gobe is produced using Chinese Hamster Ovary cells by recombinant DNA technology. The molecule contains 24 - Cys residues that are involved in 2 interchain and 10 intrachain disulfide bonds. The predominant post - translational modification includes N - linked glycosylation of the heavy chain (Asn150). The molecular weight of insulin efsitora alfa - gobe is approximately 64 kDa. ONSWIK (insulin efsitora alfa - gobe) injection is a clear and colorless to yellow solution for subcutaneous use. ONSWIK injection is a sterile, preserved formulation supplied in two concentrations (500 units/mL or 1,000 units/mL) manufactured for use in a prefilled pen. Each mL of ONSWIK U-500 contains 500 units of insulin efsitora alfa - gobe and the inactive ingredients benzyl alcohol (9 mg), dibasic sodium phosphate (0.084 mg), glycerin (17 mg), monobasic sodium phosphate (0.53 mg), phenol (1.8 mg), poloxamer 188 (0.4 mg), and Water for Injection. The 500 units/mL cartridge delivers 5 units of ONSWIK per 0.01 mL (14.3 mg/mL). Each mL of ONSWIK U-1,000 contains 1,000 units of insulin efsitora alfa - gobe and the inactive ingredients benzyl alcohol (9 mg), dibasic sodium phosphate (0.168 mg), glycerin (17 mg), monobasic sodium phosphate (1.06 mg), phenol (1.8 mg), poloxamer 188 (0.4 mg), and Water for Injection. The 1,000 units/mL cartridge delivers 10 units of ONSWIK per 0.01 mL (28.6 mg/mL). Hydrochloric acid, glacial acetic acid and/or sodium hydroxide may be added to adjust the pH. ONSWIK has a pH of approximately 6.5.
clinical_pharmacology: 12 CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 12.1 Mechanism of Action The primary activity of ONSWIK is the regulation of glucose metabolism. Insulin and its analogs lower blood glucose by stimulating peripheral glucose uptake, especially by skeletal muscle and fat, and by inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Insulin also inhibits lipolysis and proteolysis and enhances protein synthesis. The protracted time-action profile of ONSWIK results from reduced renal clearance due to its relatively large molecular size, inhibition of degradation due to binding at the neonatal Fc receptor, and reduced affinity relative to human insulin for the insulin receptor, which decreases receptor-mediated clearance. Once insulin efsitora alfa-gobe is engaged with the insulin receptor, it results in the same pharmacological effects as human insulin. 12.2 Pharmacodynamics The glucose-lowering effect of ONSWIK at steady-state was measured with a euglycemic glucose clamp study in 53 adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. The glucose infusion rate (GIR) measured in three euglycemic clamps from 0 to 24 hours, 72 to 96 hours and 144 to 168 hours post dose, along with the model-derived GIR profile show the duration of the glucose lowering effect to cover the weekly dosing interval ( see Figure 1 ). At steady-state, the mean maximum glucose-lowering effect occurred between Days 4 and 5, with a peak-trough ratio of 1.07. The glucose-lowering response was stable over the dosing interval, with low day-to-day variability of 2% (coefficient of variation for the glucose infusion rate at steady-state). The glucose-lowering effect of ONSWIK lasted approximately 4 to 6 weeks after the last weekly injection. Following a dosage adjustment, initial changes in FBG are expected within 1 to 2 weeks, with the full treatment effect of the dosage adjustment occurring in approximately 4 weeks [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 , 2.3 , 2.4 ), Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 )]. Figure 1: Pharmacodynamic Effect of ONSWIK at Steady-State Following Weekly Subcutaneous Injections of 4 units/kg Weekly Dose in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Notes: Gray dots are means and bars are standard errors of the mean glucose infusion rate (GIR). Black solid line is mean of model-predicted GIR profiles for the weekly dosing interval. Figure 1 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption Absorption of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe was evaluated in healthy subjects and adults with diabetes. Steady-state pharmacokinetics (PK) was achieved between the eighth and tenth weeks after initiating ONSWIK without a one-time starting dose and between the fourth and sixth weeks after initiating ONSWIK with a one-time starting dose of 3 times the weekly dose [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.3 , 2.4 )] . At steady-state, time to maximum insulin efsitora alfa-gobe concentration was achieved at 2.5 days post dose (Tmax). ONSWIK has a peak-to-trough ratio of 1.16 and the week-to-week variability (CV%) in total exposure of ONSWIK was 5%. The absolute bioavailability of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe after subcutaneous administration into the abdomen, was approximately 86%. Injection site (abdomen, upper arm, or thigh) did not influence the absorption or exposure of ONSWIK. Total insulin efsitora alfa-gobe exposure and maximum insulin efsitora alfa-gobe concentration increased proportionally with increasing subcutaneous doses of ONSWIK within the therapeutic dose range. No dose conversion is required if transferring a patient between the U-500 and U-1,000 strengths when each is administered at the same units/kg dose. Distribution Following a 100-unit subcutaneous bolus injection of ONSWIK, the geometric mean (CV%) volume of distribution of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (Vd) was 13 L (24%). Elimination Following a 100-unit subcutaneous bolus injection of ONSWIK, the geometric mean (CV%) clearance of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (CL) was 0.02 L/h (24%). The geometric mean (CV%) elimination half-life at steady-state is approximately 17 days (26%), independent of dose. Specific Populations No clinically significant differences in the pharmacokinetics of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe were observed based on age (18 to 88 years), sex (56% male and 44% female), race (67% White, 4.7% Black, 8.4% American Indian or Alaska Native, and 19% Asian), renal function (based on race-free CKD-EPI 2021 category) or based on alanine aminotransferase (ALT 5 to 398 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST 5 to 325 U/L). The effect of hemodialysis with kidney failure or severe hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe is unknown. Insulin efsitora alfa-gobe exposure decreased with increasing body weight (43 to 157 kg), but these effects are mitigated by the recommended dosing based on glycemic control. 12.6 Immunogenicity The observed incidence of anti-drug antibodies (ADA) is highly dependent on the sensitivity and specificity of the assay. Differences in assay methods preclude meaningful comparisons of the incidence of ADAs in the trials described below with the incidence of ADAs in other studies, including those of ONSWIK. During the 26- to 78-week treatment periods in four clinical trials in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus [see Clinical Studies ( 14 )], 59/858 (7%) of insulin-naïve and 34/1,016 (3%) of insulin-experienced adults treated with ONSWIK developed treatment-emergent anti-insulin efsitora alfa-gobe antibodies. In these trials, 30/1,874 (2%) of ONSWIK-treated adults developed anti-insulin efsitora alfa-gobe antibodies that cross-reacted with native insulin. In these trials, 23/1,874 (1%) of ONSWIK-treated adults and 23/93 (25%) of ONSWIK-treated adults with treatment-emergent anti-insuiln efsitora alfa-gobe antibodies, had estimated drug clearance that was higher than that observed in patients who were anti-insulin efsitora alfa-gobe antibody-negative. Among these 23 patients, the estimated drug clearance was approximately 5-fold higher than in patients who were anti-insulin alfa-gobe antibody-negative, and some patients had very low insulin efsitora alfa-gobe concentrations. These patients may require higher dosages of ONSWIK to achieve glycemic control [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 , 2.3 , 2.4 )] . Neutralizing antibodies against insulin efsitora alfa-gobe were detected in 18/858 (2%) of insulin-naïve and 7/1,016 (0.7%) of insulin-experienced adults treated with ONSWIK;18/59 (31%) of insulin-naïve adults and 7/34 (21%) of insulin-experienced adults with treatment-emergent anti-insulin efsitora alfa-gobe antibodies developed neutralizing antibodies. Neutralizing antibodies against native insulin were detected in 15/1,874 (0.8%) of adults treated with ONSWIK. There were no identified clinically significant effects of anti-insulin efsitora alfa-gobe antibodies on the safety of ONSWIK.

The glucose infusion rate (GIR) measured in three euglycemic clamps from 0 to 24 hours, 72 to 96 hours and 144 to 168 hours post dose, along with the model-derived GIR profile show the duration of the glucose lowering effect to cover the weekly dosing interval ( see Figure 1 ). At steady-state, the mean maximum glucose-lowering effect occurred between Days 4 and 5, with a peak-trough ratio of 1.07. The glucose-lowering response was stable over the dosing interval, with low day-to-day variability of 2% (coefficient of variation for the glucose infusion rate at steady-state). The glucose-lowering effect of ONSWIK lasted approximately 4 to 6 weeks after the last weekly injection. Following a dosage adjustment, initial changes in FBG are expected within 1 to 2 weeks, with the full treatment effect of the dosage adjustment occurring in approximately 4 weeks [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.1 , 2.3 , 2.4 ), Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 )]. pharmacokinetics: 12.3 Pharmacokinetics Absorption Absorption of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe was evaluated in healthy subjects and adults with diabetes. Steady-state pharmacokinetics (PK) was achieved between the eighth and tenth weeks after initiating ONSWIK without a one-time starting dose and between the fourth and sixth weeks after initiating ONSWIK with a one-time starting dose of 3 times the weekly dose [see Dosage and Administration ( 2.3 , 2.4 )] . At steady-state, time to maximum insulin efsitora alfa-gobe concentration was achieved at 2.5 days post dose (Tmax). ONSWIK has a peak-to-trough ratio of 1.16 and the week-to-week variability (CV%) in total exposure of ONSWIK was 5%. The absolute bioavailability of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe after subcutaneous administration into the abdomen, was approximately 86%. Injection site (abdomen, upper arm, or thigh) did not influence the absorption or exposure of ONSWIK. Total insulin efsitora alfa-gobe exposure and maximum insulin efsitora alfa-gobe concentration increased proportionally with increasing subcutaneous doses of ONSWIK within the therapeutic dose range. No dose conversion is required if transferring a patient between the U-500 and U-1,000 strengths when each is administered at the same units/kg dose. Distribution Following a 100-unit subcutaneous bolus injection of ONSWIK, the geometric mean (CV%) volume of distribution of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (Vd) was 13 L (24%). Elimination Following a 100-unit subcutaneous bolus injection of ONSWIK, the geometric mean (CV%) clearance of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (CL) was 0.02 L/h (24%). The geometric mean (CV%) elimination half-life at steady-state is approximately 17 days (26%), independent of dose. Specific Populations No clinically significant differences in the pharmacokinetics of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe were observed based on age (18 to 88 years), sex (56% male and 44% female), race (67% White, 4.7% Black, 8.4% American Indian or Alaska Native, and 19% Asian), renal function (based on race-free CKD-EPI 2021 category) or based on alanine aminotransferase (ALT 5 to 398 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST 5 to 325 U/L). The effect of hemodialysis with kidney failure or severe hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe is unknown. Insulin efsitora alfa-gobe exposure decreased with increasing body weight (43 to 157 kg), but these effects are mitigated by the recommended dosing based on glycemic control.
nonclinical_toxicology: 13 NONCLINICAL TOXICOLOGY 13.1 Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility Standard 2-year carcinogenicity studies in animals have not been performed to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe. Insulin efsitora alfa-gobe did not demonstrate higher mitogenic potential compared to human insulin as determined through in vitro assessments of receptor binding, receptor activation and cell-based functional assays. In addition, in rat and dog repeat-dose toxicity studies of up to 26 weeks duration, there were no proliferative tissue changes noted in any tissue including the mammary gland. The available nonclinical data do not indicate an increase in carcinogenic potential of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe compared to human insulin. Genotoxicity testing of insulin efsitora alfa-gobe was not performed. In a fertility study in male rats, subcutaneous injections up to 75 units/kg/week insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (up to 0.5-fold the MRHD, based on AUC) prior to and through the mating had no effect on mating performance and fertility at clinically relevant exposures at the MRHD. Similarly, mating and fertility were not adversely affected in female rats given subcutaneous doses up to 75 units/kg/week insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (up to 0.4-fold the MRHD) prior to mating through early gestation at clinically relevant exposures at the MRHD.

clinical_studies: 14 CLINICAL STUDIES 14.1 Overview of Clinical Studies The effectiveness of ONSWIK administered once weekly to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and used in combination with common noninsulin antidiabetic medications with or without mealtime insulin was evaluated in four randomized, open-label, treat-to-target, active-controlled trials. ONSWIK was studied in insulin-naïve adults using fixed-dosage titration (Trial 1) and in insulin-naïve adults using flexible-dosage titration (Trial 2), in adults previously treated with once or twice daily basal insulin (Trial 3), and in adults previously treated with daily basal and mealtime insulin (Trial 4). 14.2 ONSWIK in Insulin-Naïve Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Fixed-Dosage Titration Trial 1 (QWINT-1, NCT05662332) was a 52-week, randomized, open-label, active-controlled, treat-to-target, multinational trial that evaluated the efficacy of once-weekly subcutaneous ONSWIK in 795 insulin-naïve adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus who were inadequately controlled on one to three noninsulin antidiabetic medications with HbA1c of 7% to 10%. Patients were randomized to either once-weekly ONSWIK (N=397) or once-daily subcutaneous insulin glargine (N=398) administered according to the approved labeling. Patients remained on stable doses of one to three of the following noninsulin antidiabetic medications: Dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, biguanides such as metformin, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, oral or injectable glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, or thiazolidinediones. The mean age was 56 years, and 50% were male. The mean duration of type 2 diabetes mellitus was 9 years, and the mean BMI was 32 kg/m 2 . Overall, 68% were White, 27% were American Indian/Alaska Native, 3% were Black or African American, 1% were Asian, 0.3% were Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, and 0.5% reported multiple races; 85% identified as Hispanic or Latino ethnicity. ONSWIK was initiated at a dosage of 100 units per week and the dosage was escalated every 4 weeks, as needed, to 150, 250, then 400 units per week. Dosage adjustments were based on the median of the three most recent FBG values to achieve a target FBG range of 80 to 130 mg/dL. Patients with a dose reduction in response to hypoglycemia were not allowed to re-escalate to higher fixed doses. After week 16, patients who were treated with the 400 units per week dosage for at least 4 weeks and needed additional dosage adjustments above 400 units per week underwent subsequent dosage adjustment by 20-40 units per week as needed for glycemic control. At week 52, 18.0% of patients were on 100 units, 21.0% were on 150 units, 28.7% were on 250 units, and 8.7% were on 400 units; 23.7% of patients had undergone additional titration beyond 400 units. Insulin glargine (100 units/mL) was administered at a starting daily dosage of 10 units that was subsequently adjusted on a weekly basis by 3 to 6 units to achieve a target FBG range of 80 to 130 mg/dL and in response to hypoglycemia. At week 52, treatment with ONSWIK provided a mean reduction in HbA1c that met the pre-specified non-inferiority margin (0.4%) ( see Table 6 ). ONSWIK was initiated at a one-time starting dosage of 300 units, followed by a weekly dose of 100 units that was subsequently adjusted on a weekly basis by 20 to 40 units to achieve a target FBG range of 80 to 120 mg/dL and in response to hypoglycemia. Percent time in glucose range (%TIR,70-180 mg/dL) at baseline was 39.2% for the ONSWIK group and 38.4% for the insulin degludec group. The estimated mean change from baseline in %TIR during the last 4 weeks of the trial (Week 48 to 52) was 24.5% for ONSWIK and 21.4% for insulin degludec. Patients in China were excluded from this analysis. The primary endpoint was assessed at Week 26. The mean age was 61 years, and 56% were male. The mean duration of type 2 diabetes mellitus was 15 years, and the mean BMI was 30 kg/m 2 . For patients with a baseline FBG ≤ 120 mg/dL, a one-time starting dosage was not recommended; the initial ONSWIK dosage was the prior total basal insulin dose multiplied by 7. If there was a documented blood glucose ≤70 mg/dL in the previous week, the dose was not increased. Insulin degludec was initiated at the prior total daily basal insulin dosage then was subsequently adjusted on a weekly basis by 2 to 6 units to achieve a target FBG range of 80 to 120 mg/dL and in response to hypoglycemia. At week 26, treatment with ONSWIK provided a mean reduction in HbA1c that met the pre-specified non-inferiority margin (0.4%) ( see Table 8 ). Percent time in glucose range (%TIR,70-180 mg/dL) at baseline was 52.1% for the ONSWIK group and 52.8% for the insulin degludec group. The estimated mean change from baseline in %TIR during the last 4 weeks of the trial (Week 22 to 26) was 8.9% for ONSWIK and 8.4% for insulin degludec. information_for_patients: 17 PATIENT COUNSELING INFORMATION Advise the patient to read the FDA-approved patient labeling (Patient Information and Instructions for Use). Hypoglycemia Due to Medication Errors and Accidental Overdose Advise patients to always check the product label before each injection to confirm they are using ONSWIK and not another insulin or injectable antidiabetic medicine. Advise patients using other injectable medications for glycemic control that the dosage selection of ONSWIK differs. Instruct patients to visually verify the dialed units on the dose window of the ONSWIK KwikPen before each injection to avoid dosing errors. Instruct patients to not transfer ONSWIK from the prefilled pen to a syringe. The markings on the syringe will not measure the dose correctly and this can result in overdosage and severe hypoglycemia [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )]. Hypoglycemia Inform patients that hypoglycemia is the most common adverse reaction with insulin. Instruct patients on self-management procedures including glucose monitoring, proper injection technique, and management of hypoglycemia, especially upon initiation of ONSWIK therapy. Instruct patients on handling of special situations such as intercurrent conditions (illness, stress, or emotional disturbances), an inadequate or skipped insulin dose, inadvertent administration of an increased insulin dose, inadequate food intake, and skipped meals. [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )] . Inform patients that their ability to concentrate and react may be impaired as a result of hypoglycemia. Advise patients who have frequent hypoglycemia or reduced or absent warning signs of hypoglycemia to use caution when driving or operating machinery [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.3 )] . Hyperglycemia or Hypoglycemia with Changes in Insulin Regimen Advise patients that changes in insulin regimen can predispose to hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia and that changes in insulin regimen should be made under close medical supervision [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.4 )] . Hypersensitivity Reactions Advise patients that hypersensitivity reactions have occurred with ONSWIK. Inform patients of the symptoms of hypersensitivity reactions and to seek prompt medical attention if these symptoms occur [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.5 )] . Never Share an ONSWIK Prefilled Pen Between Patients Advise patients that they must never share an ONSWIK prefilled pen with another person, even if the needle is changed. Sharing poses a risk for transmission of blood-borne pathogens [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.7 )] . Storing the KwikPen Advise patients to store their ONSWIK KwikPen refrigerated between 2°C to 8°C (36°F to 46°F), even after first use and in between uses. The ONSWIK KwikPen may only be stored for up to a total of 14 days at room temperature not to exceed 30°C (86°F). Instruct patients to discard their ONSWIK KwikPen if kept outside of the refrigerator for a total duration over 14 days [see How Supplied/Storage and Handling ( 16 )]. spl_patient_package_insert: ONSWIK - PATIENT INFORMATION This Patient Information has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Issued: 09/2026 PATIENT INFORMATION ONSWIK ™ (ON-swihk) (insulin efsitora alfa-gobe) injection, for subcutaneous use Do not share your ONSWIK prefilled pen with other people, even if the needle has been changed. You may give other people a serious infection, or get a serious infection from them. Make sure you use the right type and dose of insulin. Always check the label on your insulin pen before each injection to avoid mix-ups with ONSWIK and other insulin products or injectable medicines used to treat diabetes. If you use another injectable medicine to treat your diabetes, pay close attention to how you select your ONSWIK dosage. The dosage of ONSWIK is different from other injectable medicines used to treat diabetes. Always make sure that you select the correct dosage of your ONSWIK KwikPen as prescribed by your healthcare provider, to avoid dosing errors and accidental overdose. People who are blind or have vision problems should not use this pen without help from a person trained to use the pen. Do not dial the maximum single dosage (400 units or 800 units) of your ONSWIK KwikPen, unless prescribed by your healthcare provider. Do not use a syringe to withdraw ONSWIK from your pen. Talk to your healthcare provider if you have any questions about how to correctly dose ONSWIK KwikPen. What is ONSWIK? ONSWIK is a long-acting man-made insulin that is used with diet and exercise to control high blood sugar in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. ONSWIK should not be used by people who have type 1 diabetes mellitus. It is not known if ONSWIK is safe and effective in children. ONSWIK is available in 2 concentrations (U-500 and U-1,000): U-500 (500 units/mL) prefilled pen can be injected in 5 unit increments and can deliver up to 400 units in a single injection. U-1,000 (1,000 units/mL) prefilled pen can be injected in 10 unit increments and can deliver up to 800 units in a single injection. Who should not take ONSWIK? Do not take ONSWIK if you: are having an episode of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). have an allergy to insulin efsitora alfa-gobe or any of the ingredients in ONSWIK. See the end of this Patient Information leaflet for a complete list of ingredients in ONSWIK. Before taking ONSWIK, tell your healthcare provider about all of your medical conditions, including if you: have liver or kidney problems. take any other medicines, especially ones called TZDs (thiazolidinediones). have heart failure or other heart problems. If you have heart failure, it may get worse while you take TZDs with ONSWIK. are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or are breastfeeding. It is not known if ONSWIK may harm your unborn or breastfeeding baby. Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. Before you start using ONSWIK, talk to your healthcare provider about low blood sugar and how to manage it. How should I take ONSWIK? Read the Instructions for Use that come with your ONSWIK KwikPen. Your healthcare provider should show you how to use ONSWIK KwikPen before you use it for the first time. Take ONSWIK exactly as your healthcare provider tells you to. Your healthcare provider should tell you how much ONSWIK to use and when to use it. Know the type, strength and amount of insulin you take. Do not change the type of insulin unless your healthcare provider tells you to. The amount of insulin and the best time for you to take your insulin may need to change If you take different types of insulin. Inject ONSWIK 1 time each week, on the same day of the week. If you need to change the day of the week, you may do so if it has been at least 4 days since your last dose. After your injection day has changed continue to inject 1 time each week on the new day you have chosen. If you miss a dose of ONSWIK: take the missed dose as soon as possible within 4 days (96 hours) after the missed dose, then continue your regular weekly dose schedule If more than 4 days have passed, skip the missed dose and take your next dose on the regularly scheduled day or take the missed dose then change your regular weekly dose schedule to start 1 week after your missed dose was injected. If you accidentally take your 1-time starting dose of ONSWIK more than 1 time (2 weeks in a row) or you take your weekly dose more than 1 time in the same week, skip your next week's dose. ONSWIK can be injected under the skin (subcutaneously) of your stomach area (abdomen), buttocks, thigh or back of the upper arms. Do not use ONSWIK in an insulin pump or inject ONSWIK into your vein (intravenously) or muscle (intramuscularly). Change (rotate) your injection sites within the area you choose with each dose to reduce your risk of getting lipodystrophy (pits in skin or thickened skin) and localized cutaneous amyloidosis (skin with lumps) at the injection sites. Do not use the exact same spot for each injection. Do not inject where the skin has pits, is thickened, or has lumps. Do not inject where the skin is tender, bruised, scaly or hard, or into scars or damaged skin. Always use a new needle for each injection to help prevent infections and blocked needles. If your needle is blocked get a new needle as instructed in the Troubleshooting section at the end of the Instructions for Use. Do not reuse or share your needles with other people. You may give other people a serious infection or get a serious infection from them. Do not use a syringe to remove the solution from the pen. Using a syringe may cause dosing errors and potential overdose. Do not dilute or mix ONSWIK with any other type of insulin or liquid medicine. Check your blood sugar levels . Ask your healthcare provider what your blood sugar levels should be and when you should check your blood sugar levels. Keep ONSWIK and all medicines out of the reach of children. What should I avoid while taking ONSWIK? While taking ONSWIK do not: drive or operate heavy machinery, until you know how ONSWIK affects you. drink alcohol or use prescription or over-the-counter medicines that contain alcohol. What are the possible side effects of ONSWIK? ONSWIK may cause serious side effects that can lead to death, including: low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Signs and symptoms that may indicate low blood sugar include: dizziness or light-headedness anxiety, irritability, or mood change confusion shakiness blurred vision slurred speech fast heartbeat sweating hunger headache severe allergic reactions (whole body reaction). Stop using ONSWIK and get medical help right away if you have any of these signs or symptoms of a severe allergic reaction: a rash over your whole body a fast heartbeat trouble breathing sweating low potassium in your blood (hypokalemia). heart failure. Taking certain diabetes pills called TZDs with ONSWIK may cause heart failure in some people. This can happen even if you have never had heart failure or heart problems before. If you already have heart failure it may get worse while you take TZDs with ONSWIK. Your healthcare provider should monitor you closely while you are taking TZDs with ONSWIK. Tell your healthcare provider if you have any new or worse symptoms of heart failure including: shortness of breath sudden weight gain swelling of your ankles or feet tiredness Treatment with TZDs and ONSWIK may need to be changed or stopped by your healthcare provider if you have new or worse heart failure. Your insulin dose may need to change because of: change in level of physical activity or exercise weight gain or loss increased stress change in diet illness other medicines you take The most common side effects of ONSWIK include: hypoglycemia, allergic reactions, reactions at the injection site, skin thickening or pits at the injection site (lipodystrophy), itching, rash, swelling of your hands and feet, and weight gain. Get emergency medical help if you have: trouble breathing, shortness of breath, fast heartbeat, swelling of your face, tongue, or throat, sweating, extreme drowsiness, dizziness, confusion. These are not all the possible side effects of ONSWIK. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088. General information about the safe and effective use of ONSWIK. Medicines are sometimes prescribed for purposes other than those listed in a Patient Information leaflet. You can ask your pharmacist or healthcare provider for information about ONSWIK that is written for health professionals. Do not use ONSWIK for a condition for which it was not prescribed. Do not give ONSWIK to other people, even if they have the same symptoms that you have. It may harm them. What are the ingredients in ONSWIK? Active ingredients: insulin efsitora alfa-gobe Inactive ingredients : benzyl alcohol, dibasic sodium phosphate, glycerin, monobasic sodium phosphate, phenol, poloxamer 188 and Water for Injection. Hydrochloric acid, glacial acetic acid and/or sodium hydroxide may have been added to adjust the pH. ONSWIK™ is a trademark of Eli Lilly and Company. instructions_for_use: ONSWIK U-500 KwikPen INSTRUCTIONS FOR USE INSTRUCTIONS FOR USE ONSWIK™ KwikPen ® [ON-swihk KWIHK-pehn] (insulin efsitora alfa-gobe) injection, for subcutaneous use 3 mL single-patient-use pen (500 units/mL, U-500) Important: ONSWIK KwikPen is used 1 time each week (once weekly). This ONSWIK KwikPen ® (Pen) works differently from other pens. It dials 5 insulin units with each click. Do not count clicks of the dose knob to select your dose. You may get too much insulin or you may not get enough insulin. Do not transfer ONSWIK insulin from your Pen into a syringe. A severe overdose can happen, causing very low blood sugar, which may put your life in danger. Know your dose of ONSWIK insulin. The Pen delivers your dose in insulin units . Insulin units may not be the same as syringe markings. Ask your healthcare provider what your dose should be for your Pen. Read this Instructions for Use before you start injecting ONSWIK KwikPen and each time you get another Pen. There may be new information. This information does not take the place of talking to your healthcare provider about your medical condition or your treatment. ONSWIK KwikPen (“Pen”) is a disposable (can be thrown away) single-patient-use prefilled pen containing 1,500 units of ONSWIK. You can give yourself more than 1 dose from the Pen. Each turn (click) of the Dose Knob dials 5 units of insulin. You can give from 5 units to 400 units in a single injection. If your dose is more than 400 units, you will need to give yourself more than 1 injection. The Plunger only moves a little with each injection, and you may not notice that it moves. The Plunger will only reach the end of the cartridge when you have used all 1,500 units in the Pen. When the Pen is empty, throw away the entire Pen and get a new Pen (see Throwing away (disposing of) Pens and Needles section at the end of this Instructions for Use). ONSWIK KwikPen is used 1 time a week. You may want to mark your calendar to remind yourself when to take your next dose. Inject ONSWIK only with your Pen. Do not transfer insulin from your Pen to a syringe. A severe overdose can happen, causing very low blood sugar, which may put your life in danger. People who are blind or have vision problems should not use the Pen without help from a person trained to use the Pen.
